analytic.title: Framework for Evaluation of Schedulability Tests for Mixed-Criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Mixed-criticality real-time system models were proven to be useful in the processes of system verification, system validation, and safety assessment in safety-critical embedded systems. In recent years, a great number of various mixed-criticality models were investigated. These models are usually accompanied with corresponding schedulability tests. In the literature, schedulability tests are typically compared following the results of evaluation on synthetically generated task sets. Due to the large number of possible test scenarios and a significant effort that needs to be undertaken to implement a certain test, it is not an easy task to reproduce these results. Furthermore, as schedulability tests are used in safety-critical systems it is crucial that tests and results are reproducible. In this paper, we present a framework for evaluation of schedulability tests and show how it can be used to reproduce the most common results.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Nowadays, there is an increased rise in the demand of embedded computers, which can execute functions with different level of importance. This is especially important in the design of safety-critical systems, which today abandons the traditional partitioned design approach in which safety and non-safety functions are executed on different computers. To avoid the increase of different computers in the system, which can increase consumption, complexity and development time, system designers nowadays use a single embedded computing platform to execute functions of different criticality, i.e., both non safety-critical and safety-critical functions. This trend increased the number of heterogeneous computing platforms, which allow onchip separation of different functions. In addition, new techniques had to be devised to maintain separation of functions with different criticality.

In the context of embedded system software, i.e., realtime operating system, the problem of partitioning and safety is linked to the scheduling of tasks, which execute functions that have different criticality. To address this and similar problems, mixed-criticality model was introduced in academia. The initial insight, which motivated extensive mixed-criticality research and publishing trend in last ten years, was given by Vestal in his seminal mixed-criticality paper [1]. The main conjecture in mixed-criticality models is that the estimation of the worst-case execution time (WCET) is linked to the importance of the function. More precisely, for critical functions, i.e., tasks, extensive rigor shall be applied for determining the execution time, which will cause the discovery of larger execution times for tasks. Mixed-criticality scheduling addresses the problem of scheduling tasks with multiple allocated WCET estimations.

A very important aspect in analysis of scheduling problems in mixed-criticality systems, but also in realtime systems in general, is determining schedulability of a task set. Therefore, in order to provide traceability and reproducibility of existing schedulability tests, we devise a framework, which enables evaluation of mixed-criticality schedulability tests.

div.head: A. Related work
div.p: As mentioned before, the first schedulability analysis of mixed-criticality systems was introduced by Vestal in [1]. His analysis targets the fixed priority preemptive mixedcriticality systems. The analysis is an extension of responsetime analysis for sporadic task sets introduced in [2]. Moreover, Vestal proposed that combining the responsetime analysis and Audsley's optimal priority assignment (OPA) [3], a priority assignment can be found for a mixedcriticality task set if it exists. This approach was shown to be optimal later by Dorin et al. [4]. In the first more comprehensive research of the fixed-priority mixed-criticality systems [5], Baruah et al. introduced the properties of runtime monitoring of execution time and static or adaptive schemes in mixed-criticality scheduling. According to these properties, the following system configurations are possible:

• static mixed-criticality denoted as SMC-NO that corresponds to the approach introduced by Vestal, • static mixed-criticality with runtime monitoring denoted as SMC, • adaptive mixed-criticality denoted as AMC, which includes runtime monitoring and two different system states.

For each static configuration, sufficient schedulability tests were devised. For adaptive scheme, two different sufficient schedulability tests were devised denoted as AMC-rtb and AMC-max. In later work, adaptive scheduling scheme was predominantly discussed in papers in both fixed-priority and dynamic priority systems [6]. A lot of dynamic scheduling tests were introduced as well, which are typically based on the earliest deadline first (EDF) with virtual deadlines scheduling in which low-criticality deadlines of highcriticality tasks are reduced in low-criticality mode [7], [8].

div.head: B. Motivation, challenge and contribution
div.p: There were attempts of enhancing the existing AMCmax schedulability tests by alternative response-time analysis denoted as AMC-IA introduced in [9]. However, the later investigation has shown that the AMC-IA test has significant errors, which when corrected did not guarantee improvement over AMC-max test [10]. Similarly, an exact schedulability test for fixed-priority mixed-criticality systems was introduced in [11]. In the later work [12], it was shown that the exact test proposed in [11] contained several errors and inconsistencies, which reduced the reproducibility of results. The framework described in this paper aims to increase reproducibility and discover similar errors in analyses.

It is important to note that we decided to devise the framework for schedulability testing in mixed-criticality systems since most of the available real-time simulation and analysis tools that are available, such as tools devised in [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], were found to be either too generic or too inflexible to efficiently compute and compare various mixed-criticality schedulability tests.

The main contribution of this paper is the framework, which aims to enable a straightforward implementation and consistent reproduction and comparison of mixed-criticality schedulability tests. In the paper, we present architecture of the framework that is written in the Java programming language. We explain how new schedulability tests can be added and how some of the most common schedulability results from the literature can be reproduced consistently. The current version of the framework is maintained in GitHub repository [18].

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this paper, we represent system as a set T of sporadic mixed-criticality tasks τ i that can be described as sets:
div.formula: τ i = { C i ,T i , D i ,L i }(1)
div.p: Vector C i in the latter equation is monotonic nondecreasing vector of WCET estimations, which correspond to WCET analyses of different rigor. Similarly, D i is monotonic non-decreasing vector of relative deadlines. Different values of deadlines are exploited in the EDF with virtual deadlines approaches. Period of each task τ i is denoted as T i . All values, including the time t, are considered to be discrete. Parameter L i denotes criticality level of a task. In this paper, we are interested in dualcriticality systems. Hence, criticality of each task can be either low (LO), or high (HI), i.e., L i ∈{LO, HI}.

The framework, which is presented in this paper, can be used for both fixed-priority schedulability tests as well as with dynamic priority assignment approaches. In addition, the framework can be used for both static and adaptive mixed-criticality schemes.

div.head: III. FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
div.p: In this section, we present code organization and specifics of the framework. In addition, we demonstrate how to implement new schedulability tests as well as priority assignment algorithms.

div.head: A. Source code organization and framework specifics
div.p: As we mentioned before, the framework is implemented in the Java programming language. The source code of the framework is organized in packages, which contain classes that implement different functionalities required for the schedulability testing. Framework packages are listed in Table I. The contents of crucial packages are shown in Tables II-VII.

Since the framework enables introduction of new schedulability tests and extension of the existing functionalities, the features that are related to the system model are implemented on a higher level of abstraction, i.e., as abstract classes and interfaces. The list of abstract classes and interfaces, which make core of the framework are shown in Table V. Three basic classes and interfaces that are specified in interfaces package, define priority assignment, feasibility test, and response time interfaces. Their respective implementations are in separate packages: package with priority assignments implementation shown in Table II, package with feasibility tests is shown in Table IV, and package with response times is shown in Table VI. Another generic item in the framework is class FeasibilityTestResponseTime, which compares the response time of each task to its respective deadline. Note that this is in line with the theoretical observation about the classes of schedulability tests, i.e., schedulability test can be either boolean test or response-time based test [19].

The evaluation package shown in Table III contains two additional classes, which are used in the experimental evaluation of schedulability tests. Class TestItem is combination of a priority assignment algorithm and a feasibility test. In the framework implementation, all fixedpriority response time analyses and feasibility tests take into an instance of TaskSet class, which contains tasks that are ordered according to a certain priority assignment. Therefore, the usage of TestItem class ensures that a task set is ordered according to the desired priority assignment prior to applying the schedulability test. However, in a special case, when using the Audsley's optimal priority assignment (OPA) the schedulability decision can be obtained in a more efficient manner. This is due to the optimality of the OPA algorithm. More precisely, when the OPA algorithm is employed, response time is utilized in the process of assigning priorities. If the OPA algorithm cannot produce a priority assignment for a task set with given response-time analysis, task set is not feasible with regard to that analysis. Note that for such an usage of a response-time analysis in the OPA algorithm, a response-time analysis has to satisfy requirements of OPA compatibility [20]. In the context of mixed-criticality systems, examples of OPA compatible schedulability tests are AMC-max, AMC-rtb, SMC-NO, SMC, and hence they can be used with the OPA algorithm. However, an exact schedulability test devised in [11] is not OPA compatible.

When the schedulability test is not OPA compatible in a fixed-priority scheduled system, it is possible to use suboptimal heuristic assignments. An example of such an assignment that is used with the exact schedulability test in [11] is implemented in our framework in class PriorityAssignmentNOPA.

Similarly, note that the usage of priority assignment is not necessary for the dynamic priority assignment approaches since the information about priority assignment is incorporated in the schedulability test itself. From the implementation point of view, it is not necessary to sort the tasks when applying feasibility tests in dynamic environment since the priority of tasks in system is not fixed, yet it changes during the system operation. Examples of such tests are tests based on the EDF with virtual deadlines approach, i.e., the EDF with virtual deadlines test devised in [21] and Ekberg's schedulability test devised in [8].

In taskgen package, implementations of task generators are placed. At the moment, a single implementation of task generator algorithm is available, i.e. UUnifast algorithm devised in [22] is implemented. However, our implementation has several additional features that are useful in the task generation:

• Implementation enables adding a constraint on the hyperperiod of the generated task sets, i.e., if the hyperperiod of generated task set exceeds the given maximum value, it shall be discarded. • Implementation enables adding a constraint, which denotes the allowed deviation of the utilization. Note that since we have to generate task sets that have integer, i.e., discrete parameters, the resulting utilization of a task set generated by the UUnifast algorithm can be different than the target utilization due to the rounding errors. • Implementation enables adding a schedulability test as a filter for the resulting task sets, i.e., an instance of IFeasibilityTest. This is especially useful in cases when we only want to observe feasible task sets with regard to a certain feasibility test. • Finally, the implementation enables blacklisting certain task sets from the generated set of task sets. This is useful when we want to generate two different sets of task sets. Class contains implementation of off-line assignment for dynamic priority system (does not change the order of tasks off-line).

div.head: B. Example of implementation of response-time analysis
div.p: In this subsection, we discuss an example of implementation of response-time analysis. For this particular example, we chose AMC-rtb analysis since it is significantly simpler than the AMC-max analysis and the exact test, but it still includes multiple system states, i.e., LO and HI, which are specific to the adaptive mixed-criticality scheme. To determine schedulability using the AMC-rtb scheme, we have to calculate the response time in low-criticality mode R i (LO), response time in high-criticality mode R i (HI), and response time in case of a criticality switch from low to high-criticality mode R i (MC). The latter response times can be calculated using the following recurrence relations:
div.formula: R i (LO)=C i (LO)+ j∈hp(τi) R i (LO) T j C j (LO) (2) R i (HI)=C i (HI)+ j∈hpH(τi) R i (HI) T j C j (HI) (3) R i (MC)=C i (HI)+ j∈hpH(τi) R i (MC) T j C j (HI) + k∈hpL(τi) R i (LO) T k C k (LO)(4)
div.p: In the latter equations, hp(τ i ) is a set of tasks with higher priority than τ i . Note that subsets hpL(τ i ) and hpH(τ i ) contain only tasks with higher priority than τ i that are low-criticality or high-criticality, respectively. div.head: C. Customizing priority assignments
div.p: Similarly, as in case of feasibility tests new priority assignments can be added. Here, we briefly illustrate how the simplest priority assignment is implemented, i.e., deadline-monotonic priority assignment (DMPA). Listing 2 shows the partial code of class that implements the DMPA assignment. Simply, by sorting a new list of tasks using the comparatorDM, which sorts tasks according to deadlines, in line 8 new priority assignment is obtained. By modifying assign method, new priority assignment algorithms can be easily added.

div.head: A. Test scenarios
div.p: In this section, we evaluate implemented schedulability tests using the framework. We evaluate the performance of the implemented schedulability tests with regard to three different parameters that are commonly analyzed in the literature. These parameters are low-criticality utilization of a task set (U (LO)), the number of tasks in a task set (n), and maximum allowed period of a task in a task set (T max ).

div.head: B. Task set generation
div.p: In the evaluation, task sets were generated using the task set generator implemented in the framework, i.e., the UUnifast algorithm implemented in class UUniFastDiscard. Specificities of the implementation were discussed in section III-A. In the evaluation of the schedulability tests, values of U (LO), n, T max were varied independently, i.e., the values of other parameters were fixed in each experiment. The complete list of input parameters and their default values for task set generation is below:
• utilization U (LO)=0.6 with δ =0.025 as allowed deviation of utilization, • the number of tasks n =6, • period T is chosen from interval [T min ,T max ]= [2, 100] with uniform distribution,
• the criticality factor CF, i.e., CF = Ci(HI) Ci(LO) =2, • and fraction of high-criticality tasks in a set CP = 0.5.

div.head: C. Results
div.p: Figs. 1234show the typical results that are often compared in the literature, which are generated here using the devised framework.

Fig. 1 shows the fraction of feasible task sets of different approaches with utilization factor in interval [0.1, 0.9]. The fixed-priority mixed-criticality schedulability tests are labeled in form RTA+PA, which denotes the pair of response-time analysis and priority assignment, e.g., AMC-rtb+OPA. Exception to this rule is EDF-VD since it is a dynamic approach, and CrMPO and DMPA assignments that are used in combination with classical non mixedcriticality response-time analysis devised in [2].

Fig. 2 shows the fraction of feasible task sets with regard to the different number of tasks in a set, i.e., n ∈ [3,8]. DMPA and CrMPO approaches are omitted due to their poor performance. Fig. 3 shows further evaluation with regard to the higher number of tasks in a set. The Exact+NOPA approach is omitted since its execution time grows exponentially when the number of tasks is increased, and therefore it cannot be computed for a large number of task sets in a reasonable time.
Finally, Fig. 4 shows the performance of tests with regard to the different period values, and these results correspond to the results in the literature as well.

V. C ONCLUSION In this paper, we presented a framework for evaluation of mixed-criticality schedulability tests that are available in literature. This task is very important today due to the significant increase in publishing of different schedulability tests and response-time analyses for mixed-criticality systems. Our framework can be used for straightforward evaluation of schedulability tests that are available in the literature. In addition, we showed how response-time analysis and priority assignments can be implemented, and we described additional features of the framework, which enable simple introduction of new tests into the framework and their evaluation. Our future work will be focused on introducing newly devised schedulability tests to the framework, and ensuring that the framework is up-to-date.
